Bufo Alvarius: The Psychedelic Toad of the Sonoran Desert — Key Connections
One-line verdict: Hamilton Morris’s updated edition of the 1984 classic, now including a detailed NaBH4 reductive amination protocol for 5-MeO-DMT that serves as a direct chemical benchmark for the Paradisi group’s enzymatic cascade.
Why This Matters
Glenn’s group published a bi-enzymatic cascade to 5-MeO-tryptamine (ACS Catalysis 2025), making this text a concrete comparison point: the traditional chemical synthesis of the final N,N-dimethylation step that the enzymatic route aims to replace. The purification discussion (solvent switching, acid-base extraction, recrystallization, short-path distillation) maps directly onto downstream processing challenges in flow biocatalysis. The text also feeds into the Web of Psychedelics project as a primary source on Bufo alvarius venom chemistry and the conservation argument for synthetic 5-MeO-DMT.
Key Ideas
1. NaBH4 reductive amination at low temperature avoids Pictet-Spengler cyclization
The core synthetic insight: running reductive amination below 20 C with NaBH4 (instead of NaBH3CN) avoids beta-carboline side products because the borohydride intercepts the iminium intermediate faster than the competing intramolecular Pictet-Spengler cyclization can close the ring.
Connects to: Hitchhikers_Guide_to_Flow_Chemistry — the flow chemistry review discusses Pictet-Spengler reactions and temperature control in continuous flow, where precise thermal management is inherently easier than in batch.
Connects to: paradisi_group_context — the group’s enzymatic route bypasses the selectivity problem entirely: tryptophanase (EcTnaA) and tryptophan decarboxylase (RgnTDC) produce 5-MeO-tryptamine without needing reductive amination or temperature-dependent selectivity control.
2. NaBH3CN leaves persistent cyanide-containing trace impurities
Morris reports that even after column chromatography and recrystallization, NaBH3CN-derived products retain cyanide-smelling impurities (likely amino-cyanoborane adducts or N-cyanomethyltryptamines). This is a practical safety and purity argument for switching reagents.
Connects to: paradisi_group_context — this impurity problem is one of the strongest arguments for biocatalytic routes: enzymes produce no cyanide-containing byproducts, and the aqueous reaction medium simplifies purification.
3. 5-Methoxytryptamine can be prepared from melatonin via base-catalyzed deacetylation
The text describes a route from melatonin (widely available sleep supplement) to 5-methoxytryptamine using NaOH in isoamyl alcohol at reflux, with sodium dithionite as reductant.
Connects to: Glossary — melatonin appears in the psychedelics glossary as a biosynthetic precursor in the tryptamine pathway, and the vault’s Huberman notes cover melatonin’s circadian role.
New territory — the melatonin-to-tryptamine chemical conversion has no existing vault coverage. Could be worth a short note in _RESEARCH/ comparing this chemical deacetylation to the enzymatic route using deacetylases.
4. Solvent switching via selective MeOH evaporation enables extraction
After reaction in MeOH (miscible with both water and organics), the MeOH is boiled off selectively (BP 64 C vs 100 C for water) until the remaining aqueous phase is polar enough for liquid-liquid extraction with EtOAc. The key is stopping at ~10% MeOH rather than going to dryness, to avoid the product crashing out as intractable tar.
Connects to: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis_ Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study — the Paradisi group’s own paper on solvent switching in continuous flow, which addresses the same fundamental problem (moving from aqueous enzymatic conditions to organic workup) but in a flow context using membrane separators rather than batch evaporation.
5. Acid-base extraction selectively isolates amines from complex mixtures
The purification relies on pulling the freebase amine into 3N HCl (protonates the amine, making it water-soluble), washing away neutral impurities in the organic phase, then basifying and re-extracting. This exploits the pKa difference between the target amine and neutral/acidic byproducts.
Connects to: paradisi_group_context — the group’s pipeline includes purification of amine products from enzymatic reactions. Acid-base extraction is directly applicable to isolating tryptamine products from biocatalytic cascades, since amino acid substrates (zwitterionic) stay in the aqueous phase while freebase amine products partition into organic solvent.
6. Short-path vacuum distillation as a scale-up purification strategy
For large-scale work, the text recommends short-path distillation over recrystallization to avoid vast solvent quantities. 5-MeO-DMT freebase boils at 160-170 C at 0.6 mm/Hg. The discussion extends to wiped-film and thin-film evaporators for thermally sensitive indoles.
Connects to: Hitchhikers_Guide_to_Flow_Chemistry — the flow chemistry review covers continuous downstream processing including in-line distillation, which connects to the residence-time-at-temperature principle that makes WFE preferable to batch distillation for sensitive compounds.
7. Water concentration must stay below 10% to maintain solvent amphiphilicity
A practical rule: too much water causes tryptamine freebases to precipitate as intractable tar that traps stir bars and resists redissolution. The MeOH/water ratio must preserve amphiphilicity so both polar NaBH4 and nonpolar tryptamine stay in solution.
New territory — no existing vault notes cover solvent system design for tryptamine solubility. The principle (balancing polar/nonpolar solubility in a single phase) is relevant to buffer optimization in enzymatic tryptamine synthesis.
8. Conservation argument: synthetic production protects wild toad populations
The synthesis appendix was added to the 6th edition explicitly to reduce harvesting pressure on Bufo alvarius. Morris frames synthetic 5-MeO-DMT as both greener and more sustainable than toad-derived material.
Connects to: DMT — the DMT substance page covers the natural occurrence of tryptamines in plants and animals, and the broader question of natural vs synthetic sourcing.
Connects to: HamiltonMorris133 — Gallimore and Morris discuss the vision for self-sufficient chemical synthesis infrastructure to reduce dependence on natural sources.
9. TLC monitoring with 4:1 MeOH:EtOAc resolves tryptamine intermediates
The Rf order (5-MeO-T < 5-MeO-NMT < 5-MeO-DMT < 6-MeO-THBC) provides a practical analytical handle for reaction monitoring. The text notes a better system: pure ethanol or methanol with 1% triethylamine.
New territory — no vault notes cover TLC conditions for tryptamine analysis. Relevant if the Paradisi group needs to monitor tryptamine cascades by TLC in addition to HPLC/MS.
10. Formaldehyde addition rate must exceed NaBH4 addition rate
Because the NaBH4 solution is more concentrated (1.57 mol/100 mL vs 1.34 mol/100 mL for formaldehyde), the formaldehyde must be added faster to prevent excess borohydride from reducing formaldehyde to methanol before it can condense with the amine. This is a kinetic competition for the same electrophile.
Connects to: paradisi_group_context — analogous to substrate feeding strategies in enzymatic cascades, where the ratio of substrates fed to a multi-enzyme system determines selectivity. The group’s flow reactors use residence time and feed ratios to control exactly this type of competing-pathway problem.
Connection Map

Cross-Domain Bridges
Research to Creative: The Paradisi group’s enzymatic tryptamine cascade (research) directly addresses the conservation problem Morris raises (creative/psychedelics). The group’s ACS Catalysis paper is, in effect, the academic answer to the question this pamphlet poses: how to make tryptamines sustainably without chemical waste or toad harvesting. This is a rare case where Glenn’s research program and his psychedelics interest project converge on the same molecule.
Synthesis to Phenomenology: The purification challenges (colored impurities from indole oxidation, beta-carboline side products) are not just synthetic nuisances. Beta-carbolines like pinoline are themselves psychoactive (MAO inhibition), meaning impure 5-MeO-DMT would produce pharmacologically different experiences than pure material. The purity discussion connects directly to the phenomenological mapping in NOTES_5-MeO-DMT_intranasal_phase1, where dose-response precision depends on compound purity.
Open Questions

Could the Paradisi group’s tryptophanase/decarboxylase cascade be extended with a methyltransferase to go all the way to 5-MeO-DMT (not just 5-MeO-tryptamine), eliminating the need for any chemical N-methylation step?
What is the actual logP difference between 5-MeO-DMT and DMT (without the methoxy group), and how does this quantitatively affect extraction efficiency from aqueous biocatalytic reaction mixtures?
Are the beta-carboline side products (pinoline, N-methyl-pinoline) that form during Pictet-Spengler cyclization pharmacologically relevant contaminants in toad-derived 5-MeO-DMT preparations?

04_REFERENCES/Movie-and-Documentary/NOTE.content:
The Supercomputers Designing the Future of Psychedelic Science | VICE | Blueprint: Key Connections
One-line verdict: A visually strong documentary that links ergot biology, LSD pharmacology, and computation-led ligand discovery, with its greatest value lying in the bridge between psychedelic history and the machinery now producing new chemical space.
Source confidence: Medium. The film gives direct access to relevant scientists, laboratory work, receptor structures, and field observations, but it mixes these with autobiographical and speculative material without citations or a clear boundary between established results and personal belief.
Why This Matters
The existing LSD page tells the substance’s chemical, cultural, and political story, while this source shows the research pipeline that now follows from that history: fungal biosynthesis, receptor structure determination, medicinal chemistry, and virtual screening. It also supplies the undeveloped bridge already noted in Fungal-Biocat-Wildcard-Lanes between fungal secondary metabolism and the Web-Of-Psychedelics project. For the Experiential Monism work, it offers a more precise mechanistic layer beneath the broad constraint-loosening account in 04_Psychedelics, while also showing why receptor engagement alone cannot stand in for phenomenology.
Key Ideas
1. The LSD-bound 5-HT2A receptor has become a design object
The documentary presents an active-state LSD-bound 5-HT2A structure resolved at atomic scale. Once the ligand-binding geometry and receptor conformation are visible, psychedelic chemistry can move from analogue-making around known scaffolds toward structure-guided design.
Connects to: LSD: the page currently stops at 5-HT2A agonism and modern neuroimaging, so this adds the next stage in the scientific history, direct structural access to the receptor-ligand complex.
2. Binding kinetics may separate potency from duration
David Nichols proposes that LSD-like ligands may remain potent because they become trapped in the receptor, and that avoiding this trapping could yield high-potency compounds with shorter action. The source presents this as a drug-design hypothesis, not an established therapeutic result.
Connects to: LSD: its listed 8 to 14 hour duration becomes a molecular design variable rather than merely a descriptive feature of the experience.
3. Virtual screening reverses the order of medicinal chemistry
Brian Roth describes computationally docking a virtual library of billions of drug-like molecules against 5-HT2A and using the receptor model to select novel scaffolds for synthesis. The important shift is from synthesizing first and testing second to searching chemical space computationally before committing laboratory effort.
Connects to: HamiltonMorris005: the head-twitch response supplies a downstream functional assay, while structure-based screening supplies an upstream generator of candidates. Together they expose the full gap between receptor fit, receptor activation, animal behaviour, and human experience.
4. One receptor can support several pharmacological regimes
The documentary juxtaposes 5-HT2A activation by psychedelics with therapeutic receptor blockade in schizophrenia. That contrast makes the receptor a control point whose effect depends on direction, signalling bias, circuit context, and dose, rather than a simple psychedelic switch.
Connects to: The Psychedelic Model of Schizophrenia (1976): the older psychotomimetic model tried to map psychedelic states onto schizophrenia at the level of whole syndromes, whereas current receptor pharmacology gives a narrower and more testable point of comparison.
Connects to: HamiltonMorris005: lisuride and the limits of the head-twitch assay already show that 5-HT2A binding or agonism does not uniquely determine a hallucinogenic outcome.
5. Receptor engagement is not yet an account of experience
Structural biology can explain how a molecule stabilizes an active receptor state, but not by itself how this becomes altered selfhood, perception, or meaning. The documentary repeatedly crosses this explanatory gap without resolving it.
Connects to: 04_Psychedelics: the receptor structure constrains the chemical beginning of the proposed loosening process, but the note’s attractor and subject-formation account operates at a different explanatory scale. Neither level can substitute for the other.
6. Ergot chemistry is a fungal ecological strategy before it is a human drug source
The film frames ergot alkaloids as likely defenses against insects and other ecological competitors. Human psychoactivity is therefore an incidental consequence of shared neurotransmitter systems across animals, not evidence that the compounds evolved for human consciousness.
Connects to: LSD: this corrects the substance page’s human-centered origin story by placing the lysergamide scaffold inside fungal ecology before Hofmann’s semisynthesis.
7. A branch point in biosynthesis produces different ergoline families
The account identifies chanoclavine aldehyde as a branch point separating dihydroergot alkaloid producers from lysergic acid derivative producers. The broader lesson is that modest enzymatic changes in a conserved fungal pathway can redirect the chemical family that emerges.
Connects to: Fungal-Biocat-Wildcard-Lanes: the note already treats pathway reconstruction, enzyme localization, and substrate scope as design variables for fungal bioactives. This gives that programme a specific branch-point example in the LSD lineage.
8. Fungi contain chemically silent biosynthetic capacity
The researchers describe genomes containing complete or near-complete alkaloid pathways even when the corresponding chemistry is not observed under ordinary growth conditions. Inducing or reconstructing those pathways turns fungal genomes into maps of latent chemical space.
Connects to: Fungal-Biocat-Wildcard-Lanes: this supports the distinction between discovering a pathway genetically and making it operate as a usable biocatalytic system, including the host, compartment, expression, and process constraints that follow.
9. The apparent producer may not be the true producer
When an ergoline appears in a plant or animal, the documentary suggests that a symbiotic fungus may be the actual biosynthetic source. This shifts natural-product attribution from the visible organism to the full host-microbe system.
Connects to: Fungal-Biocat-Wildcard-Lanes: the fungal postdoc direction is strongest when fungi are treated as hidden chemical infrastructure across ecological systems, not merely as isolated production organisms.
10. Prohibition changed the material infrastructure of research
The source shows that legal and commercial unavailability of controlled compounds made a small number of licensed chemists essential to landmark receptor and clinical studies. The research interruption was therefore not only ideological. It also removed compounds, suppliers, and practical continuity.
Connects to: LSD: the existing account describes the psychedelic winter as scientific silence, while this source shows the supply-chain mechanism by which that silence was enforced and later reversed.
Connects to: The Psychedelic Model of Schizophrenia (1976): both sources show how institutional conditions determine which hypotheses can remain experimentally alive.
11. Exploratory synthesis and hypothesis testing are distinct discovery modes
Nichols characterizes Shulgin’s practice as open-ended chemical exploration, asking what happens if a molecule is made, while academic pharmacology requires explicit hypotheses and assays. The contrast is useful because modern virtual screening industrializes the exploratory mode but still needs biological tests to convert novelty into knowledge.
Connects to: HamiltonMorris005: the head-twitch assay illustrates both the power and danger of the testing layer. It can rank receptor-active compounds well, yet it cannot answer what the resulting state is like or whether subjective effects matter therapeutically.
Connects to: Web-Of-Psychedelics: the project already separates chemists, substances, concepts, and historical actors. This source shows that their interactions, rather than any one category, are the actual engine of the field.
Connection Map

Cross-Domain Bridges
The strongest bridge is between Fungal-Biocat-Wildcard-Lanes and Web-Of-Psychedelics. The former already identifies ergot and psilocybin pathways as a fungal biocatalysis lane but leaves the adjacent cultural project undeveloped. This documentary supplies the missing middle: ecological function, biosynthetic branching, licensed synthesis, receptor structures, and computational redesign form one continuous story from fungus to experience.
A second bridge joins HamiltonMorris005 and 04_Psychedelics. The animal-assay note warns that receptor-level behavioural proxies cannot recover subjective experience, while the Experiential Monism note models the experience at the level of constraint and attractor dynamics. The documentary makes the need for both levels unusually visible, but does not provide evidence that the phenomenological model is uniquely correct.
Open Questions

Which active-state 5-HT2A features predict hallucinogenic signalling rather than generic agonism, and can that distinction survive testing across genuinely novel scaffolds?
How much of the described virtual-screening programme has produced published functional or behavioural data, rather than promising receptor fits?
Can the ergot pathway’s branch points and ecological diversity be mined systematically for useful enzymes or scaffolds without making the controlled end products the only research target?

04_REFERENCES/Movie-and-Documentary/Oran.title: Orange Sunshine
04_REFERENCES/Movie-and-Documentary/Oran.content:
Hybrid documentary with archival footage, present day interviews, and a few reenactments.
First person memory carries the story, there is little outside narration.

Timeline

John Griggs took LSD for the first time after robbing it from an actor in Hollywood. The trip made him want to change his life and begin a mission to turn on the world.
His friends and all their girlfriends formed the The Brotherhood of Eternal Love
The group moved to Modjeska Canyon. An old church became a sanctuary. Spiritual books circulated and practice grew.
They flew to Europe, rented cars, and drove to Afghanistan to buy hash from the Tilkai brothers. Hidden steel compartments were welded, shipments routed through Seattle, the money supported the scene.

News came that John Griggs had died. The center was gone and the mood shifted.
Coordinated pre-dawn sweeps followed. Large seizures and named labs appeared in the news. People scattered across borders. The story meets the War on Drugs and Scheduling of Drugs era.

Sacrament and crime appear together, the film lets both frames stand.
Ease of movement in that era shaped events, flights were simple, borders were light, smuggling looked easy.
Community came first, a shared belief held the group together

04_REFERENCES/Movie-and-Documentary/The-.content:
Overview
The Sunshine Makers (2015), directed by Cosmo Feilding-Mellen, son of Amanda Feilding of the Beckley Foundation, tells the intertwined story of Tim Scully and Nicholas Sand, two chemists driven by a messianic belief that LSD could transform human consciousness.
After his first psychedelic experience, Scully became convinced that mass enlightenment could be achieved through chemistry. Meeting Timothy Leary and other figures at Billy Hitchcock’s estate, he connected with Sand and together they resolved to synthesize and distribute pure LSD to as many people as possible.

The Orange Sunshine Era
Through Hitchcock’s network they acquired lysergic acid, the precursor for LSD, shipped via the Bahamas and Miami to California. In November 1968, they built a clandestine lab and began producing what became known as “Orange Sunshine”, regarded as the purest and most widespread acid ever made.
They operated almost continuously, work, sleep, synthesize, repeat. Distribution was handled by the The Brotherhood of Eternal Love, a spiritual-communal network led by Mick Randal, moving millions of doses across the globe, including India, Europe, and Vietnam.
They envisioned a “psychedelic nation”, believing that 200 kilograms of LSD would catalyze planetary awakening, “green grass in Manhattan.”

Idealism and Collapse
Both chemists saw LSD as a spiritual technology, not a drug. Nicholas Sand described their mission as “chemists on a mission from God.” Scully focused on purity and precision, believing science could serve enlightenment.
But the wave soon turned. Owsley Stanley, famous for the Wall of Sound and early LSD synthesis, was identified by authorities as a central figure in the acid underground. As social unrest deepened, LSD became illegal in California (1966) and later federally banned under the 1967 Drug Abuse Control Act, setting the stage for Nixon’s War on Drugs in 1971.
The pair relocated their labs to Denver, but chemical suppliers in Berkeley betrayed their trail. Federal agents traced shipments and arrested Scully in 1969.

The Fall of the Psychedelic Nation
Nicholas Sand remained at large, evading surveillance despite mounting IRS pressure. His obsession consumed his personal life, his partner left him as he established a new lab in St. Louis, even as the broader movement decayed into amphetamine, heroin, and biker-gang chaos.
A water leak led police to his hidden lab while he was away. Meanwhile Billy Hitchcock, arrested for tax fraud, turned state witness, implicating both chemists.
Scully was sentenced to 20 years, Sand to 15, and in a surreal twist they ended up cellmates.

Inside Prison
Sand’s girlfriend Nancy Pinney smuggled LSD into the prison, allowing the pair to continue “sessions” with other inmates, some accounts claim the drug even entered the food supply.
Scully abstained, dedicating himself to study. He completed a PhD in Psychology, earning early parole after 10 years.
Sand escaped with Pinney to Canada, continuing underground synthesis for another two decades. He was eventually arrested in 1996, tried by the same judge (Conti), and sentenced again, this time marking the end of a 30-year cycle of LSD production.

Legacy
After release Scully moved into computer science and consciousness research, living quietly with his wife. Sand served six years, later teaching about spirituality and alchemy until his death in 2017.
The documentary balances archival footage, modern interviews, and psychedelic animation, contrasting idealism and pragmatism, spirit and system, portraying a movement that believed chemistry could liberate the mind, only to collide with the machinery of law and order.

Dosed (2019) – follows a woman using psilocybin and ibogaine for addiction recovery, shows the tension between underground therapy and medicalization.

The Mind, Explained: Psychedelics (2019, Netflix) – short episode, neat overview of serotonin systems, modern trials, and Michael Pollan’s perspective.


How to Change Your Mind (2022, Netflix) – adapts Pollan’s book, each episode covers one substance: LSD, psilocybin, MDMA, mescaline.


Neurons to Nirvana (2013) – broader overview, interviews with researchers and therapists including Rick Doblin, Stanislav Grof, and Amanda Feilding.

Hoffman’s Potion (2002) – vintage footage and interviews with Albert Hofmann, Stanislav Grof, and early LSD researchers.


A New Understanding: The Science of Psilocybin (2015) – calm, clinical style, hospice trials and the return of psilocybin therapy.


The Substance: Albert Hofmann’s LSD (2011) – European documentary, connects Hofmann’s discovery to the cultural and political fallout.


Dirty Pictures (2010) – intimate portrait of Alexander Shulgin, mixing chemistry, philosophy, and domestic scenes in his home lab.


The Secret History of LSD (2020, CBC) – focuses on CIA, MK-Ultra, and military programs that paralleled the counterculture wave.

DMT: The Spirit Molecule (2010) – based on DMT - The Spirit Molecule by Rick Strassman, blends experiment footage, interviews, and early CGI “entity” visuals.

04_REFERENCES/Paper/Convention-on-Psycho.title: Convention on Psychotropic Substances (1971)
04_REFERENCES/Paper/Convention-on-Psycho.content:
Overview
The Convention on Psychotropic Substances was adopted in Vienna on 21 February 1971.
It was convened by the United Nations Economic and Social Council to establish international control over synthetic and natural psychotropic substances not covered by the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs.
The Convention defines a system of four Schedules (I–IV) grouping substances according to their potential for abuse, public health risk, and recognized medical value.
Each State Party agrees to restrict use to medical and scientific purposes and to prevent diversion into illicit traffic.

Intent and Scope
Preamble:

Concern for public health and social problems caused by abuse of psychotropic substances.
Recognition that such substances are indispensable for medicine and science but require control.
Determination that international cooperation and coordination are necessary.

Implementation:

Each Party must enact national measures to enforce the provisions of the Convention (Art. 22).
The World Health Organization (WHO) evaluates substances and recommends scheduling (Art. 2 § 4).
The Commission on Narcotic Drugs (CND) decides on additions, transfers, or deletions (Art. 2 § 5).
Substances may be placed in Schedule I, II, III, or IV depending on their abuse potential, health risk, and medical usefulness.
Traditional or religious use of certain plants may be reserved by States at ratification (Art. 32 § 4).


The Four Schedules
Schedule I
Strictest control.
Use limited to scientific and very restricted medical purposes under direct government supervision (Art. 7).
Examples: lysergide (LSD), DMT, psilocybine, mescaline, MDMA, THC (early form).
Measures include:

prohibition of non-scientific use
special licensing and recordkeeping
export/import only by competent authorities


Schedule II
Controlled substances with recognized medical application but high risk of abuse.
Examples: amphetamine, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, phencyclidine.
Measures include:

manufacture and trade under licence (Art. 8)
medical prescriptions required (Art. 9)
import/export authorizations (Art. 12)


Schedule III
Moderate control, lower risk of dependence, accepted therapeutic use.
Examples: buprenorphine, flunitrazepam, pentobarbital, cathine.
Measures include:

licensing and record requirements (Arts. 8–11)
prescriptions as determined nationally (Art. 9)


Schedule IV
Lowest control.
Mild abuse potential, wide medical application (mainly sedatives and anxiolytics).
Examples: benzodiazepines (diazepam, alprazolam), barbiturates, phenobarbital.
Measures include:

records for manufacture and international trade (Art. 11)
prescription and labelling standards (Art. 10)
prohibition of public advertising (Art. 10 § 2)


National and International Administration

Each Party should maintain a special administrative authority for implementation (Art. 6).
The WHO provides medical–scientific assessments.
The CND decides on scheduling changes by two-thirds majority (Art. 17 § 2).
The International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) monitors compliance and may request explanations or recommend embargoes (Art. 19)


Enforcement

Parties must treat intentional violations as punishable offences (Art. 22).
States may adopt stricter measures than required (Art. 23).
Measures include inspection, licensing, recordkeeping, import/export control, and reporting to the INCB (Arts. 8–16).


Entry into Force

Open for signature until 1 January 1972.
Entered into force 90 days after 40 ratifications (Art. 26).
States may denounce the Convention after two years (Art. 29).
Applies to all territories under the jurisdiction of each Party unless excluded by notification (Art. 27).

Uber die Synthese des Bufotenin-methyl-athers (5-Methoxy-N-dimethyl-tryptamin) und Bufotenins
Authors: Toshio Hoshino and Kenya Shimodaira
Journal: Annalen der Chemie, Vol. 520, 1936, pp. 221-224
Series: Synthesen in der Indol-Gruppe, XV
Summary
First total synthesis of bufotenin methyl ether (5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine, now known as 5-MeO-DMT) and its conversion to bufotenin (5-hydroxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine). Part of a broader program on indole alkaloid synthesis connected to the eserine (physostigmine) problem.
Synthetic Route
Starting material to bromide

5-Methoxy-indolyl-3-acetonitril hydrolyzed to 5-methoxy-indolyl-3-acetic acid (mp 146-147 C)
Esterification to the ethyl ester (mp 97-98 C)
Bouveault-Blanc reduction (Na/EtOH) to 5-methoxy-tryptophol (bp 194 C/4 mm)
Bromination with PBr3 in ether to 5-methoxy-indolyl-3-ethyl-beta-bromide

Bromide to 5-MeO-DMT

Reaction with 33% dimethylamine in methanol, sealed tube, 100 C, 16 h
Acid-base extraction, vacuum distillation (bp 208-210 C/4 mm)
Crystallization from ether/petroleum ether: colorless prisms, mp 66-67 C

5-MeO-DMT to bufotenin

O-Demethylation with AlCl3 in benzene, 100 C, 15 h
Acid-base workup, ether extraction
Identity confirmed by mixed melting point of dipikrate (mp 177-178 C) and monopikrate with authentic bufotenin from the ethyl ether route

Alternative route via quaternary salt

Exhaustive methylation of 5-methoxy-tryptamine with MeI/Na2CO3 in ethanol (>90% yield of trimethylammonium iodide, mp 183 C)
Conversion to chloride via AgCl exchange (mp 144 C)
Hofmann elimination by high-vacuum pyrolysis at 240-250 C to yield 5-MeO-DMT (confirmed by pikrate mp 174-175 C)

04_REFERENCES/Paper/NOTES_Hoshino_Shimod.content:
Hoshino & Shimodaira (1936): First Synthesis of 5-MeO-DMT and Bufotenin
One-line verdict: The 1936 paper that proved the structure of bufotenin and 5-MeO-DMT by total synthesis, establishing the synthetic chemistry foundation for an entire class of psychoactive tryptamines.
Source confidence: High. Peer-reviewed synthetic chemistry with full experimental characterization, melting point comparisons against authenticated natural products, and elemental analysis. The gold standard of structural proof for its era.
Why This Matters
This is the origin point for synthetic access to 5-MeO-DMT and bufotenin. Every subsequent pharmacological, phenomenological, and therapeutic study of these compounds (including the intranasal 5-MeO-DMT clinical trial in NOTES_5-MeO-DMT_intranasal_phase1) depends on the structural certainty this paper established. For the Web of Psychedelics, this fills a gap: the project documents the pharmacology and phenomenology of tryptamines, but not their synthetic history. This paper is the earliest synthetic landmark for the 5-MeO-DMT/bufotenin pair.
Key Ideas
1. First total synthesis of 5-MeO-DMT via an indole alkylation route
Hoshino built the molecule from 5-methoxyindole-3-acetic acid through a four-step sequence: hydrolysis, esterification, Bouveault-Blanc reduction to tryptophol, bromination, then nucleophilic displacement with dimethylamine. This “bromide + amine” strategy became the template for tryptamine synthesis for decades.
Connects to: Tryptamines (Web of Psychedelics substance class). This paper is the first synthetic entry for the tryptamine class, predating Shulgin’s systematic exploration by 60 years. The Tryptamines page currently lacks historical synthesis context.
Connects to: Glossary (entry on 5-MeO-DMT). The glossary describes 5-MeO-DMT as “naturally occurring” from toad secretions and plants. This paper adds the synthetic dimension: it was made in a lab in 1936, before its role as a psychoactive compound was even recognized.
2. Structural proof of bufotenin by synthesis
By converting synthetic 5-MeO-DMT to bufotenin via AlCl3 O-demethylation and confirming identity with Wieland’s natural isolate (matching pikrate melting points), Hoshino proved bufotenin’s structure unambiguously. Before this, the structure was only inferred from degradation studies.
Connects to: Glossary (entry on Anadenanthera, which mentions bufotenine from plant seeds). Hoshino’s synthesis closed the loop: degradation told you what pieces the molecule contained; synthesis proved how they were assembled.
3. The quaternary ammonium salt route as an alternative pathway
Exhaustive methylation of 5-methoxy-tryptamine with methyl iodide gave the trimethylammonium salt in >90% yield. Hofmann elimination by vacuum pyrolysis then gave 5-MeO-DMT. This is notable because it showed two independent routes to the same product, strengthening the structural proof.
Connects to: HamiltonMorris133 (discussion of INMT enzyme converting tryptamine to DMT). The biological N-methylation of tryptamine mirrors what Hoshino did chemically with methyl iodide. Manske’s observation that chemical methylation gives a hard-to-separate mixture of mono-, di-, and trimethyl products is the synthetic chemist’s version of the selectivity problem that INMT solves enzymatically.
4. Manske’s concurrent work revealed the difficulty of selective tryptamine methylation
R.H. Manske (Canada) showed that reacting tryptamine with methyl iodide gives an inseparable mixture: monomethyl, dimethyl, trimethyl, and recovered starting material. Selective N-methylation of tryptamine is hard because each successive methyl group barely changes nucleophilicity.
Connects to: Glossary (entries on 4-AcO-DMT, 4-HO-MET, 5-MeO-MiPT and other N-substituted tryptamines). Shulgin’s later solutions to the selectivity problem (using different amines rather than sequential methylation) are downstream of the challenge Manske documented here.
5. Connection to the physostigmine (eserine) synthesis program
Hoshino’s tryptamine work was not aimed at psychoactive compounds at all. It was a stepping stone toward synthesizing physostigmine, the cholinesterase inhibitor from Calabar beans. The psychoactive properties of bufotenin and 5-MeO-DMT were incidental to the original research goal.
New territory: No existing vault note covers the physostigmine connection or the broader history of indole alkaloid synthesis programs in the 1930s. Consider a note in _CREATIVE/Web_Of_Psychedelics/02_HISTORY/ on the accidental origins of tryptamine synthesis.
6. Tryptophol as a key synthetic intermediate
The route goes through 5-methoxy-tryptophol, the alcohol analog of tryptamine. This intermediate is biologically relevant: tryptophol is a natural product found in fungi and fermented foods, produced by yeast from tryptophan via the Ehrlich pathway.
Connects to: Paper-Strategy (BiocatMiner). The Paper Strategy discusses RgTDC tryptophan decarboxylase as making biogenic amines (tryptamine, tyramine). Hoshino’s chemical route to tryptamine derivatives parallels the enzymatic route: both start from an indole building block and functionalize the sidechain. The enzymatic path (decarboxylation) is more direct than Hoshino’s (acid to ester to alcohol to bromide to amine).
7. Identity confirmation by “mixed melting point”
The structural proof depended on a now-obsolete technique: mixing synthetic and natural samples and checking that the melting point did not depress. This was the 1930s equivalent of spectroscopic comparison, predating NMR by two decades.
New territory: No vault note covers pre-spectroscopic structural elucidation methods. For a history-of-chemistry note, this is a good example of how structural certainty was achieved before modern instrumentation.

Cross-Domain Bridges
Chemistry (research) to phenomenology (EM/creative): Hoshino synthesized 5-MeO-DMT as a structural proof exercise with zero awareness of its psychoactive properties. The compound that 04_Psychedelics describes as producing “dramatically reduced internal constraint” and that NOTES_5-MeO-DMT_intranasal_phase1 maps phenomenologically was, at birth, just an intermediate on the road to physostigmine. This is a striking example of how the chemical and experiential descriptions of the same molecule can be completely disconnected for decades.
Synthetic chemistry to biocatalysis (research): Hoshino’s 4-step route from indole acetic acid to tryptamine derivative is exactly the kind of transformation that enzymatic approaches now accomplish in a single step. The tryptophan decarboxylases in Glenn’s Chlamydomonas biocatalysis project are the biological solution to the problem Hoshino solved the hard way.
Open Questions

When was 5-MeO-DMT first recognized as psychoactive? Hoshino clearly did not know. Somewhere between 1936 and the first pharmacological reports, someone made the connection.
Did Hoshino’s group ever complete the physostigmine synthesis that motivated this entire indole series? The paper is Part XV; the target may have been reached in a later installment.
The Tryptamines page in Web of Psychedelics is empty. Should this paper anchor a historical synthesis timeline for the tryptamine class?

04_REFERENCES/Paper/The-Psychedelic-Mode.title: The Psychedelic Model of Schizophrenia — The Case of N,N-Dimethyltryptamine
04_REFERENCES/Paper/The-Psychedelic-Mode.content:
Authors: J. Christian Gillin, Jonathan Kaplan, Richard Stillman, Richard J. Wyatt
Published: [American Journal of Psychiatry, 133 (2): 203–208 (1976)  ](- 10.1176/ajp.133.2.203)
Affiliation: National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), St. Elizabeths Hospital, Washington D.C.

Overview

The paper reviewed all research on N,N-Dimethyltryptamine (DMT) as a possible endogenous psychotomimetic—a “schizotoxin” that might explain schizophrenia through internal overproduction of hallucinogenic tryptamines.
It was the culmination of two decades of “transmethylation” research following Stephen Szára’s early DMT studies (1950s) and the discovery of trace DMT in human tissue.
The authors systematically applied a set of criteria (adapted from Koch’s postulates) to evaluate whether DMT met the requirements of a disease-causing agent.


Main Findings

Psychoactive validity: Confirmed that DMT produces strong, short-lived psychedelic effects in humans similar to LSD or mescaline.
Endogenous presence: Acknowledged sporadic detection of DMT in blood and urine, but no consistent elevation in schizophrenic patients.
Biochemical feasibility: Recognized that enzymes such as indolethylamine N-methyltransferase (INMT) exist in human tissue and can synthesize DMT in vitro, but in-vivo synthesis was not demonstrated conclusively.
Tolerance and pharmacology: Showed incomplete tolerance and extremely rapid metabolism—factors that made DMT an unlikely cause of chronic psychosis.
Conclusion: While biochemically plausible, DMT failed to meet key criteria for a schizophrenia model; the theory was described as “plausible but unproven.” The authors recommended giving the hypothesis “a decent burial.”


Tone and Subtext

The review was written by federal researchers during the early U.S. War on Drugs, a time when psychedelic research faced political pressure and shrinking funding.
Its rhetoric—judicial, conclusive, even funerary—served to close the DMT-as-schizotoxin line of inquiry, aligning with institutional efforts to end psychedelic studies rather than encouraging further exploration.
The phrase “a decent burial” effectively performed a bureaucratic dismissal, signaling that the topic was scientifically settled and no longer fundable.
This stance contrasts with the classical scientific ethos: falsified or unsupported hypotheses normally invite new experiments, not programmatic abandonment. The data themselves—endogenous presence, enzymatic synthesis, rapid clearance—were fertile leads that could have opened new biochemical or neuropharmacological questions.


Historical Impact

The paper became the definitive “closure document” of the endogenous psychosis era. After its publication, most DMT and tryptamine studies ceased within government institutions.
When Rick Strassman revived DMT research in the 1990s, he cited this review as emblematic of how political climate, not data quality, froze an entire scientific field.
In retrospect, the review is both a rigorous summary and a case study in scientific gatekeeping—illustrating how institutional context can shape what is considered “finished science.”

04_REFERENCES/Podcast/HamiltonMorris005.title: HamiltonMorris005
04_REFERENCES/Podcast/HamiltonMorris005.content:
“This podcast is the first of what I hope to be a series of “journal club” discussions with scientists about an important scientific paper. In this episode Jason Wallach and I discuss the strange origin of the head twitch response and how it became the most important behavioral correlate for 5HT2A agonism in non-human animals.”
Overview
Hamilton and Wallach go through the old LSD mouse papers — the origin of the Head-Twitch Response (HTR) — and how it became the main behavioral marker for 5-HT2A activation.
The discussion quickly goes beyond just the data, asking how we can even measure a psychedelic effect, what animal models actually tell us, and whether the subjective experience itself is necessary for therapy.

commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Head-twitch_response_induced_by_a_psychedelic_drug_in_mice.webm
Notes

The 1956 paper is bizarre for modern science. it reads like something from the 18th century — no methods, no strain information, no statistics. they just write things like 10–60% of mice twitched.
still, it’s the first report of LSD producing a distinct behavioral response in animals.
LSD (5–100 µg IV) caused a fast head shake within 5–10 minutes, lasting up to 2 hours.
mescaline, yohimbine, serotonin — no effect.
they tried random follow-up experiments:

indole before LSD made the twitch permanent in 5–30% of mice
isolation for 2–3 weeks then regrouping made ~80% show the effect for weeks
reserpine suppressed it while given, then it came back
both researchers were not from that field and never continued, probably unaware how important their finding was


LSD was still used mainly as a psychotomimetic, a model for psychosis.

The HTR today

the head-twitch response is still common in research, used as an indicator for 5-HT2A receptor activity
a 2020 paper by Halberstadt et al. quantified it across many substances and found very strong correlations:

mouse HTR potency vs human hallucinogenic dose: r = 0.9448 (n = 36)
HTR vs rat drug-discrimination potency: r ≈ 0.95 for LSD-trained rats, r ≈ 0.96 for DOM-trained rats


in other words, the mouse HTR ED50 predicts human hallucinogenic potency with high accuracy across classic psychedelics.
examples of HTR ED50 values (mice):
LSD ≈ 52.9 µg/kg
DOM ≈ 1.75 µmol/kg
DMT ≈ 10 mg/kg
these values match well with the corresponding human dose ranges (micrograms to hundreds of milligrams).
the HTR dose–response is often non-monotonic, rising and then decreasing at higher doses, likely due to 5-HT2C modulation of 5-HT2A output.
false positives / negatives:

Lisuride is a 5-HT2A agonist but not hallucinogenic and fails to produce HTR — shows functional selectivity.
metabolism and mixed receptor activity can also interfere with interpretation.



What are we even modelling?

we have no idea what it’s like to be a mouse.
even if you could see a “movie” of its experience, you’d still interpret it through human thinking.
to truly understand it, you’d have to become the mouse.
so what are we actually modelling?
the HTR only shows that a drug activates the receptor — not what the experience is like.
the same problem exists for human disorders like major depression.
diagnoses are based on symptoms, not unified biology.
two people can both “have depression” but be completely different physiologically.
rating scales are rough tools — they rely on interpretation and self-report.
it’s strange to expect a mouse swimming test or head-twitch model to map neatly onto human emotional experience.

Psychological vs biological

reduction of experimental conditions to purely physiological causes feels too simplistic and denies any psychological dimension.
psychedelics might be the weird exception here — the “delusional” quality itself can change perspective, which might be why they help.
studies where drug-naive people rate the importance of their psychedelic experience show it often ranks among the top five experiences of their lives.
how could that not be relevant to mental health outcomes?
these are not magic bullets, but they can reset perception and outlook.
with proper guidance, that shift might sustain itself.
you cannot separate the psychological from the biological.
one influences the other constantly.

Back to the mouse model

even if you could somehow see what the mouse experiences, you’d still analyse it through your own cognition.
there’s no equivalent to a “head-twitch” in humans.
false positives or negatives can occur due to metabolic differences between species, or due to how the behavior is defined.
for instance, Lisuride is active in receptor binding assays but produces no HTR, while some compounds may twitch but lack hallucinogenic activity
the dose–response curve of HTR is bell-shaped, which matches the discussion in the podcast — lower doses trigger HTR strongly, higher doses reduce it again.

Therapy and subjectivity

can the subjective experience be removed and still keep the therapeutic effect? maybe partially.
ketamine shows it might work to some degree.
but completely ignoring the experience seems wrong — it’s part of what creates meaning and reorganization.
people often describe psychedelic experiences as moments of seeing life “through another lens.”
it’s not everything, but probably a necessary part of the process.
psychedelics are not one-size-fits-all drugs. each compound has its own therapeutic profile, and will need its own approach — something Alexander Shulgin already said decades ago.

Other points

Forced Swim Test: absurd on the surface, but still predicts antidepressant activity, even for ketamine. it’s reliable because of statistics, not realism.
neuroplasticity is probably the shared mechanism.
depression involves prefrontal atrophy from chronic stress.
psychedelics reopen those circuits for repair — the intense, confusing subjective state might be the conscious side of that process.
MDMA for PTSD: shows how subjective experience and biology intertwine.
MDMA allows trauma recall without fear, leading to memory reconsolidation and new emotional associations.
it wouldn’t work the same way without that felt safety.

Main takeaway
the head-twitch response is a translational model. it measures receptor-level potency, not experience. it’s useful but limited — and reminds us that psychedelic therapy can’t be reduced to pharmacology alone. to measure psychedelics, you need to include the subject too.

“You’d have to become a mouse to understand the mouse.”


References

Keller & Umbreit (1956) “Permanent Alteration of Behavior in Mice by Chemical and Psychological Means.” Science 124, 123–124.
Halberstadt AL et al. (2020) “Correlation between the potency of hallucinogens in the mouse head-twitch response assay and their behavioral and subjective effects in other species.” Neuropharmacology 164, 107933.

04_REFERENCES/Podcast/HamiltonMorris133.content:
The Hamilton Morris Podcast
POD 133: Dr. Andrew Gallimore on DMTx and the DMT Island
A long, far-ranging discussion with chemist and neuroscientist Dr. Andrew Gallimore about his continuous DMT infusion project (DMTx), his book Death by Astonishment, and his broader vision for psychedelic research beyond government control.
Websites:

www.buildingalienworlds.com
www.noonautics.org
www.eleusismind.com


Dr. Andrew Gallimore — Key Points

Plans for a psychedelic island dedicated to DMT research, designed to operate independently from government bureaucracy.

Possible futures: a utopia of open research for the enlightened wealthy, or a cult-like nightmare?


Noonautics as the overarching framework for extended DMT exploration.
The island would serve both as a research center and retreat, with infrastructure for self-sufficient chemical synthesis and design of new psychoactive compounds.
Visitors could observe the chemistry behind the experiences, like a “psychedelic microbrewery.”
Discussion of the Kafkaesque bureaucracy surrounding psychedelic research approval.
The extended-state DMT (DMTx) system aims to maintain subjects in continuous immersion, offering new insight into the structure of the DMT realm.
Mentions MXE in relation to altered-state pharmacology.


Philosophical Reflections

Morris asks if people who already hold non-physicalist worldviews handle the intensity of DMT better.

Gallimore answers that belief in spirits or demons offers no protection — such frameworks can collapse even harder when confronted with DMT’s deeper realities.
( a rather simplistic, top-down view — especially for those who never actually took it.)


Mentions a “baker review” suggesting DMT might play a protective role for the brain, supporting Rick Strassman’s hypothesis that DMT release might preserve neural integrity during near-death states.
Notes an enzyme (INMT) converting tryptamine to DMT, said to be inhibited by a short peptide found in rabbit brain/blood.


Historical Context — DMT’s Discovery

1852: Richard Spruce drinks ayahuasca (caapi) but not enough for a full visionary effect.
For over a century, scientists struggled to identify the active compound behind this “gateway to the spirit world.”
1956: Stephen Szára isolates and identifies DMT as the active molecule, previously thought to be harmala alkaloids or bufotenin.
1950s: William Burroughs travels to Colombia seeking yage (Ayahuasca) and discovers Chacruna as the DMT-containing plant.
Homer Pinkley, a student of Richard Schultes, later receives much of the credit.
Researchers initially found DMT orally inactive, only understanding it a decade later when the role of MAO inhibitors was uncovered.
Dennis McKenna later demonstrated that combining DMT with MAO inhibitors (harmala alkaloids) made it orally active — confirming earlier hypotheses about ayahuasca.
1978: American ethnobotanist Jeremy Bigwood tested this by ingesting 100 mg DMT freebase with a similar dose of harmaline, confirming the synergistic effect.
